title: Modi Receives the FAO's Highest Honour in Rome — and Dedicates It to India's 110 Million Farmers
excerpt: The Agricola Medal recognises India's food security transformation under Modi's tenure. For the diaspora, it is a reminder of how far the country's agricultural story has come since the famines their grandparents remember.
body:
In the wood-panelled Plenary Hall of the Food and Agriculture Organization's Roman headquarters — a building whose history stretches back to Mussolini's Italy — Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday received the Agricola Medal, the UN agency's highest honour. FAO Director-General QU Dongyu placed the medal and called it recognition of Modi's "invaluable contribution and long commitment to the wellbeing of India, and all people."

Modi, characteristically, redirected the spotlight. "This medal belongs to the annadatas of India," he said, using the Hindi word for food-givers — a term that encompasses the 110 million smallholder farmers who receive direct income support under the PM-KISAN scheme, the fishermen who have benefited from expanded blue economy investments, and the livestock workers who form the backbone of rural India's protein supply chain.

## A Record Worth Examining

The FAO's citation was specific. It highlighted India's food-based safety net — the world's largest, covering 800 million people since the COVID-19 pandemic through the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana. It noted the direct benefit transfers to farmers, the national push for regenerative and natural farming, and India's successful campaign to have 2023 declared the International Year of Millets. It praised Modi's use of India's G20 presidency to position digital public infrastructure as a global public good — a framework that has since been adopted by the African Union and several Southeast Asian governments.

The numbers behind these initiatives are substantial. India's foodgrain production has risen from 252 million tonnes in 2014-15 to an estimated 330 million tonnes in 2025-26. The country has gone from being a net importer of pulses to approaching self-sufficiency. Soil health cards have been issued to more than 230 million farmers, and micro-irrigation coverage has expanded by 75 percent since 2015.

## The Historical Thread

Modi's acceptance speech drew a line from the present back to two figures whose names the Indian diaspora may recognise but whose contributions are often overlooked. Binay Ranjan Sen served as FAO Director-General from 1956 to 1967 — the first head of a UN agency from a developing country — and established the World Food Programme during his tenure. M.S. Swaminathan, the architect of India's Green Revolution who passed away in 2023, spent years at FAO shaping global food policy. Modi's invocation of both men was deliberate: a reminder that India's relationship with global food governance is not new, even if the current scale of its domestic programmes is unprecedented.

## What NRIs Hear

For the Indian diaspora — many of whom grew up hearing family stories of food scarcity, ration cards, and the anxieties of a country that depended on PL-480 wheat shipments from America — the Agricola Medal carries emotional weight that transcends policy metrics. The transformation from a country that could not feed itself to one that feeds 800 million through its safety net in a single generation is, by any measure, extraordinary.

The ceremony in Rome was attended by ambassadors, UN agency heads, and Indian nationals working across the Rome-based food agencies — IFAD, WFP, and FAO itself. Many of them represent a quiet but significant strand of the Indian diaspora: development professionals who have spent careers working on the very food security challenges their own country has now, at least in the FAO's assessment, substantially overcome.

Critics will note what the medal does not address: the ongoing distress among small and marginal farmers, the controversy over agricultural market reforms, and the fact that India still ranks 105th on the Global Hunger Index. But in the ornate halls of FAO's Roman headquarters, on a Wednesday afternoon in May, the recognition was for what has been achieved — and the annadatas to whom Modi, with some justification, dedicated it.
